section_summary: This section documents mounting pressure in October–November 1940 for stronger U.S. restrictions on exports of strategic materials to Japan, including petroleum, copper, iron, steel, mercury, weapons and industrial technology. It combines diplomatic and intelligence reporting with public and congressional correspondence, especially concerning Japanese attempts to obtain supplies through Latin America and Europe. A substantial group of memoranda and statistical attachments examines Chilean copper sales, their importance to Chile’s economy and the anticipated U.S. copper shortage, while other papers assess how embargoes might affect Japanese policy and expansion in China and Southeast Asia.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on suspected indirect gasoline shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records discussion of a Tokyo report alleging Japanese efforts to acquire high-octane gasoline through South America.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine and Yost discuss a Tokyo telegram; shipments to South America are watched for possible transshipment of gasoline to Japan.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram no. 1049 on indirect gasoline purchases
subfiles.about: Reports an allegation that Japan was seeking American high-octane gasoline through South American intermediaries.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo telegram 1049: a Polish colleague believes Japan is critically short of high-octane gasoline; reliability unconfirmed.

subfiles.title: Louis Ludlow letter forwarding a San Francisco complaint
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter and clipping from San Francisco concerning exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Ludlow forwards a San Francisco complaint on continued American shipments useful to Japan, not as criticism.

subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping: “War Materials for Japan”
subfiles.about: Describes scrap metal, copper and petroleum cargoes departing West Coast ports for Japan near the effective date of the scrap embargo.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: the scrap-iron restriction stopped only a small part of war materials reaching Japan, citing cargoes of scrap copper and oils on the Bordeaux; locals want controls extended.

subfiles.title: George N. Winchell note questioning continued shipments
subfiles.about: Questions why strategic shipments to Japan continued despite the announced embargo.
subfiles.summary: George Winchell's note asks why reported San Francisco shipments were allowed when an embargo supposedly existed.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Louis Ludlow
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Winchell material and supplies regulations and a White House statement on scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Ludlow for forwarding George N. Winchell’s clipping concerning iron, steel, copper scrap and oil exports to Japan. He encloses the September 30 and July 2 regulations and the September 26 White House statement, retains a copy of Winchell’s letter and returns the original.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s instruction for reply to William G. Lennox
subfiles.about: Directs that an appropriate reply be drafted to an attached letter.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary asks Hornbeck to arrange a reply for his signature to William Lennox's criticism of Japan policy.

subfiles.title: William G. Lennox letter urging an embargo
subfiles.about: Urges prompt embargoes on essential war materials to Japan and on imports of Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Lennox, with years in East Asia, is aghast at delay in imposing economic restrictions, warning Asians read hesitation as fear.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to William G. Lennox
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Lennox’s views concerning the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Welles notes Lennox's October 9 letter and appreciates the spirit in which he wrote.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s instruction for reply to Mrs. McBride
subfiles.about: Orders preparation of a reply to an influential Cleveland correspondent.
subfiles.summary: Welles asks Hornbeck to draft an appropriate response. He describes Mrs. McBride as exceptionally intelligent and influential in Cleveland.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Malcolm L. McBride letter advocating economic pressure on Japan
subfiles.about: Calls for broad economic restrictions on Japan and comments on American policies toward China, Spain and Europe.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. McBride reports steel figures considering a Japanese offer for 50,000 tons of iron ore, argues exports sustain Japan's war, urges embargoes and a ban on silk, and criticizes policy toward Spain.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to Mrs. McBride
subfiles.about: Acknowledges McBride’s letter and the enclosed articles on Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Welles says the broad and far-reaching issues raised cannot be answered in detail by letter. He welcomes McBride’s views, offers to discuss them if she visits Washington and says the material has been shown to other interested State Department officers.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s instruction for reply to the Kempner letter
subfiles.about: Requests a draft response to the attached Kempner letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles asks Hornbeck to prepare a reply to the Kempner letter, which supports a broader embargo on materials useful to Japan and other Axis powers.

subfiles.title: Harris L. Kempner letter proposing a comprehensive embargo
subfiles.about: Supports Welles’s Cleveland address and urges coordinated embargoes and Anglo-American naval cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Kempner recommends coordinated restrictions on copper, petroleum, pig iron and steel with Britain, Canada, Australia and the Dutch, and U.S. access to Singapore in exchange for bombers and bombsight technology.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to Harris L. Kempner
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Kempner’s policy recommendations and compliment on Welles’s Cleveland address.
subfiles.summary: Welles says Kempner's October 9 views were carefully considered and thanks him for praising the September 28 Cleveland address.

subfiles.title: Warren A. Seavey letter forwarding a Far East proposal
subfiles.about: Forwards a policy proposal said to represent the views of a group of Harvard colleagues.
subfiles.summary: Seavey sends Hornbeck a Far East action proposal, with a note that the contributors substantially share the position.

subfiles.title: “The Far East: A Proposal for Action”
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and the Department of State
subfiles.about: Proposes embargoes, large-scale aid to China and U.S. use of Singapore to check Japanese and Axis expansion.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: Japanese domination of China and the South Pacific would imperil the U.S. and others; it recommends cutting off strategic materials and credits, aiding Chiang, and arranging use of Singapore.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of Seavey’s proposal
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the proposal for action in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Seavey for his September 20 letter and enclosure, read with interest.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on increased Japanese purchases of pig iron and steel
subfiles.about: Reports industry concern that Japan was replacing prohibited scrap imports with pig iron and manufactured steel.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Barringer says Japanese purchases of pig iron and steel rose sharply, including 150,000 tons of ship plate, and objects that scrap is barred while finished products from scrap are not.

subfiles.title: Coast Guard forwarding memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards Coast Guard communications intelligence concerning Japanese-American trade.
subfiles.summary: Covell transmits a Coast Guard summary of commercial messages on copper, lead, cobalt, tungsten and steel for Saugstad.

subfiles.title: Summary of Japanese-American commercial communications
subfiles.about: Summarizes intercepted messages arranging shipments of strategic metals and steel.
subfiles.summary: Summary of messages on large purchases of electrolytic copper, lead, cobalt and tungsten with irrevocable credit via Manzanillo or California, and a request to arrange steel; source rated reliable.

subfiles.title: Instruction to acknowledge Gerald M. Fennell’s letter
subfiles.about: Directs the Division of Far Eastern Affairs to acknowledge an attached letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles sends the correspondence to Hamilton for an appropriate acknowledgment. The attached Fennell letter urges stronger action against Japan.

subfiles.title: Gerald M. Fennell letter urging immediate action against Japan
subfiles.about: Calls for stopping gasoline, copper and coke exports and confronting Japanese expansion before Japan grows stronger.
subfiles.summary: Fennell urges the U.S. to act first by cutting strategic exports and fighting from Singapore and Darwin if needed, warning delay lets Japan add battleships and seize the Dutch East Indies.

subfiles.title: Maxwell M. Hamilton reply to Gerald M. Fennell
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Fennell’s letter and enclosed newspaper article on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton, for Welles, tells Fennell his letter and clipping are noted and his spirit appreciated.

subfiles.title: Filing instruction on the Fennell correspondence
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs file
subfiles.about: Records Hamilton’s direction that a letter be filed.
subfiles.summary: Filing instruction noting Hamilton's endorsement File MMH on the Fennell correspondence.

subfiles.title: Gerald M. Fennell life-insurance solicitation to Hamilton
subfiles.about: Solicits Hamilton’s interest in a life-insurance trust convertible to retirement income.
subfiles.summary: Gerald Fennell solicits Hamilton about a life-insurance trust and asks to call to discuss it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Mexican scrap-iron assurance
subfiles.about: Points to Ambassador Daniels’s report that Mexican government scrap sales would not be destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Daniels's October 23 Mexico despatch: assurance on sales of Petroleos Mexicanos scrap iron.

subfiles.title: Despatch on sale of scrap iron by Petróleos Mexicanos
subfiles.about: Reports efforts to prevent Mexican petroleum scrap from reaching Japan or another totalitarian power.
subfiles.summary: Commercial attaché reports negotiations on 19,000 tons of Petroleos Mexicanos scrap; Moss promised not to sell it to Japan, but the attaché relies on a contract ban and Mexican Treasury export control, with Finance Minister Suarez's cooperation.

subfiles.title: Scanlan Corporation inquiry on sale of Japanese patent rights
subfiles.about: Asks whether U.S. regulations prohibit selling Japanese rights to an oil-shale extraction process.
subfiles.summary: Scanlan Corporation explains its process removes oil from shale but isn't refining, and asks where in Los Angeles or San Francisco it can get regulatory information.

subfiles.title: Madrid telegram no. 595 on mercury and arms purchases
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese purchases of Spanish mercury, pistols and ammunition for shipment through Montevideo and Lisbon.
subfiles.summary: Madrid telegram 595: Mitsui bought another 2,250 flasks of mercury via Montevideo, and Japanese buyers got 1,300 pistols and 750,000 cartridges from Guernica for Tianjin via Lisbon.

subfiles.title: Lansdale G. Sasscer letter forwarding Eisenberg’s appeal
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent letter urging an immediate embargo on materials exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Sasscer sends B. N. Eisenberg’s letter to the Department for consideration. He characterizes the enclosed constituent communication as self-explanatory.

subfiles.title: B. N. Eisenberg letter advocating immediate embargoes
subfiles.about: Urges immediate restrictions on scrap iron, petroleum, pig iron, cotton and other war supplies exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: B. N. Eisenberg compares U.S. trade with Japan to Britain's prewar sales to Germany and asks Sasscer to press for immediate embargoes.

subfiles.title: Department of State acknowledgment to Sasscer
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Eisenberg’s letter and says raw-material exports to Japan are under interagency consideration.
subfiles.summary: State thanks Sasscer for Eisenberg's views, says the issue is studied with other agencies, and returns the letter.

subfiles.title: Corrected Peiping telegram no. 408 on responses to U.S. pressure
subfiles.about: Transmits an informant’s argument for sustained economic pressure until Japan withdraws from China and abandons southward expansion.
subfiles.summary: Peiping telegram 408: an informant welcomes the steel and scrap ban, urges stopping all trade until Japan changes policy, and warns most of superficial concessions meant to divide American opinion.

subfiles.title: Earlier copy of Peiping telegram no. 408
subfiles.about: Preserves a less complete copy of the telegram assessing possible Japanese reactions to American restrictions.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the informant’s endorsement of the steel and scrap ban and the analysis of three possible Japanese courses. Several passages are garbled or missing, prompting requests for repetition, while the distribution notes record repetition to Chungking and Shanghai and transmission of code text to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum denying a general moral embargo on copper
subfiles.about: States that no general commercial or moral embargo on U.S. copper exports to Japan was then in effect.
subfiles.summary: Note denying a general moral embargo on copper: companies might cut exports commercially, but there was no real curtailment to Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on Chilean copper shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Mr. Daniels, Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: Records a meeting with copper executives about surging Japanese purchases of Chilean copper and possible safeguards for hemispheric defense.
subfiles.summary: Copper executives say Japanese orders from Chile more than doubled after U.S. supplies were curtailed; Welles suggests short contracts with a priority clause for U.S. and Chilean defense, amid a looming U.S. copper shortage.

subfiles.title: Braden copper deliveries, January–September 1940
subfiles.about: Tabulates 1940 copper deliveries by month and destination.
subfiles.summary: Table of Braden electrolytic copper deliveries, January-September 1940, to Italy, Japan, Sweden and other markets.

subfiles.title: Braden copper deliveries for 1939
subfiles.about: Provides monthly figures for Braden’s 1939 copper deliveries.
subfiles.summary: Table of Braden electrolytic, three-star and Bessemer copper deliveries by month in 1939, a baseline for 1940 changes.

subfiles.title: Anaconda memorandum describing three Chilean copper statements
subfiles.from: Cornelius F. Kelley, Anaconda Copper Mining Company
subfiles.about: Explains attached statements on payments to Chile, lost export markets and Japanese copper commitments.
subfiles.summary: Anaconda memorandum describing three statements: copper subsidiaries' contribution to Chile's economy, lost markets under the British blockade, and commitments to deliver Chilean copper for Japanese account.

subfiles.title: Chile Exploration Company dollars transferred to Chile
subfiles.to: Anaconda Copper Mining Company and Department of State
subfiles.about: Details dollar transfers for plant requirements and Chilean taxes in 1939 and the first nine months of 1940.
subfiles.summary: The schedule lists monthly transfers under Chilean laws 5169 and 6334 and calculates annual and grand totals. It documents the company’s dollar contributions to Chile through operating expenditures and tax payments.

subfiles.title: Andes Copper and Potrerillos Railway dollar transfers to Chile
subfiles.from: Andes Copper Mining Company and Potrerillos Railway Company
subfiles.to: Anaconda Copper Mining Company and Department of State
subfiles.about: Lists dollar transfers to Chile for plant needs and income taxes from January 1939 through September 1940.
subfiles.summary: The two-page schedule provides monthly figures under Chilean tax laws and consolidated totals for the two companies. It also identifies taxes payable during 1940 and supports the argument that copper operations were important to Chile’s economy.

subfiles.title: Statement of copper proceeds and transfers returned to Chile
subfiles.to: Anaconda Copper Mining Company and Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes dollars, supplies, taxes and exchange-rate benefits accruing to Chile from copper operations.
subfiles.summary: Statement of copper proceeds returned to Chile in 1939-1940, with estimates, taxes, and the peso gain to the Chilean government from preferential exchange.

subfiles.title: Braden Copper Company statement of proceeds returned to Chile
subfiles.to: Anaconda Copper Mining Company and Department of State
subfiles.about: Presents Braden’s actual and estimated financial contribution to Chile through September 1940.
subfiles.summary: Braden Copper statement of plant transfers, taxes and materials placed in Chile, with projections and the exchange-rate profit to the Chilean government.

subfiles.title: Consolidated Chilean copper-company financial totals
subfiles.about: Consolidates financial figures for company transfers, taxes, copper proceeds and exchange effects in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Degraded table consolidating 1939-1940 dollar and peso payments connected with Chilean copper production.

subfiles.title: Detailed Braden schedule of transfers and taxes
subfiles.to: Anaconda Copper Mining Company and Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides monthly detail supporting Braden’s totals for plant transfers and Chilean tax categories.
subfiles.summary: The schedule lists monthly 1939 and January–September 1940 transfers for plant requirements and several tax categories. The facing totals show how each payment contributed to the annual grand totals and identify taxes due around November 15.

subfiles.title: Foreign copper deliveries from Chile and Andes, January–September 1940
subfiles.from: Chile Exploration Company and Andes Copper Mining Company
subfiles.to: Anaconda Copper Mining Company and Department of State
subfiles.about: Tabulates 1940 Chilean copper deliveries by destination country.
subfiles.summary: Table of Chilean and Andes copper deliveries to European, Asian and South American destinations in early 1940, showing rapid growth in Japanese deliveries.

subfiles.title: Foreign copper deliveries from Chile and Andes for 1939
subfiles.from: Chile Exploration Company and Andes Copper Mining Company
subfiles.to: Anaconda Copper Mining Company and Department of State
subfiles.about: Lists monthly copper deliveries by destination for 1939.
subfiles.summary: Table of 1939 Chilean and Andes copper deliveries, with Japan far below its 1940 level.

subfiles.title: Copper contracted for Japanese account at New York and Chile
subfiles.about: Lists contracts, tonnage, ships and delivery schedules for copper sold to Mitsui and Mitsubishi for Japanese account.
subfiles.summary: The schedule records 14,412 tons for delivery from the New York area and 10,451 tons for delivery in Chile. It identifies buyers, contract and order numbers, named Japanese vessels, delivery dates and, for New York shipments, loading arrangements at Perth Amboy.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the domestic copper position
subfiles.about: Forecasts U.S. and Anaconda copper supplies, consumption and deficits through June 1941.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum estimates stocks and production for the final four months of 1940 and anticipates that domestic consumption could rise to roughly 105,000 tons per month in early 1941. It projects an industry deficit of about 57,000 tons and an Anaconda deficit of about 38,600 tons during the first half of 1941. It concludes that American fabricators may require 20,000–25,000 tons of foreign copper each month, in addition to material used for export fabrication.

subfiles.title: Leon Henderson letter returning copper statistics
subfiles.about: Returns twelve statistical documents concerning American copper producers in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Leon Henderson thanks Welles and returns the copper statistics left by American copper company representatives.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles letter transmitting copper statistics
subfiles.about: Sends twelve Chilean copper documents to Henderson for temporary examination.
subfiles.summary: Welles sends Henderson twelve tabular documents left by American copper companies in Chile and asks that he return them.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese interest in gasoline-plant plans
subfiles.about: Records Morito Morishima’s inquiry about export-license applications for gasoline-plant plans and specifications.
subfiles.summary: Morishima asks about Universal Oil Products' applications to export plant designs under its 1928 and 1938 Japan Gasoline contracts; Moseley says they are under the Export Control Administrator's consideration.

subfiles.title: British Embassy memorandum on Japanese shortages and strategic intentions
subfiles.about: Summarizes conversations about Japanese reserves, shortages, fears and likely expansion into Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy memo: Mori reportedly said Japan has two years of scrap but lacks special metals and gasoline and fears a silk boycott; Baeyens says Germany urges Japanese action in Indochina and Southeast Asia.

subfiles.title: Confidential memorandum on Japanese mercury accumulation
subfiles.about: Concludes that Japan was urgently accumulating mercury and assesses global production and supply routes.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: Japan was buying U.S. and Mexican mercury for use or war reserves as British limits cut Spanish and Italian supplies; Axis buying could dominate the Western market. Statistics continue beyond this section.
